title: Risers
analyses: Effective tension and bending moment analysis
Internal pressure, temperature and flow-induced loading analysis
Extreme storm and accidental disconnection analysis
Riser fatigue life and integrity assessment
scope: Applicable to steel catenary risers, top-tensioned risers, flexible risers, hybrid risers and drilling risers.

models.text: The suite should implement Newton's second law, Lagrange's equations of motion, conservation of linear and angular momentum, static equilibrium, Euler–Bernoulli beam theory, Timoshenko beam theory, Kirchhoff rod theory, Cosserat rod theory, nonlinear cable equations, catenary equations, elastic rod formulations, geometric stiffness relationships, effective tension formulations, large-displacement beam theory and nonlinear finite-element formulations.

The suite should include Airy wave theory, Stokes wave theory, Morison's equation, hydrodynamic added-mass and damping models, current drag, wave-current interaction, potential-flow vessel hydrodynamics, response amplitude operators, vessel six-degree-of-freedom motion models and nonlinear vessel–riser coupled dynamics.

The suite should incorporate Strouhal vortex shedding relationships, reduced velocity formulations, hydrodynamic lift and drag coefficients, wake oscillator models, Van der Pol oscillator representations, modal VIV response models, empirical response amplitude and frequency relationships, cross-flow and in-line VIV prediction, multimode excitation models and stochastic current-profile assessment.

Relevant methods include nonlinear seabed contact, Winkler soil springs, Coulomb friction, elastic–plastic soil deformation, cyclic seabed stiffness degradation, pipe penetration resistance, suction and uplift resistance, touchdown-zone hysteresis and nonlinear contact–separation formulations.

The suite should employ shell buckling theory, Brazier ovalization, external pressure collapse models, combined axial tension–bending–pressure interaction, fracture mechanics, S–N curves, rainflow counting, Palmgren–Miner damage, spectral fatigue, Dirlik's method, stress concentration factors and nonlinear local cross-sectional analysis.

Models should include deployment catenary analysis, dynamic vessel–riser interaction, tensioner stiffness, buoyancy-controlled configuration, lifting dynamics, transient disconnect modelling, emergency drift-off response and nonlinear contact-impact analysis.

The suite should integrate geometrically nonlinear finite-element riser models with vessel hydrodynamics, mooring dynamics, seabed contact, fatigue calculations and flow-induced vibration. Hybrid frequency-domain/time-domain approaches, modal VIV calculations combined with time-domain vessel motions, global–local finite-element submodelling, CFD-derived hydrodynamic coefficients and reduced-order surrogate models should be supported where suitable.

inputs.text: Total length, outside diameter, inside diameter, wall thickness, segmented geometry, bend-stiffener length, buoyancy distribution and hang-off coordinates.
Steel catenary, top-tensioned, hybrid, lazy-wave or other riser configuration, including connection geometry and support arrangement.
Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, density, yield strength, tensile strength, fatigue properties and corrosion allowance.
Fluid density, internal pressure, temperature, flow rate, fluid composition and operating transients.
Water depth, current velocity profiles, wave spectra, seawater density and extreme storm conditions.
Vessel position, displacement, draft, six-degree-of-freedom motion time histories, motion RAOs and mooring-related offsets.
Hang-off angle, top tension, connection stiffness, vessel offsets and rotational restraints.
Seabed profile, soil stiffness, friction properties, embedment behaviour and cyclic soil resistance.
Normal and tangential drag, added mass, inertia coefficients, current direction and VIV parameters.
Buoyancy element dimensions, submerged weight, distribution, stiffness and attachment position.
S–N curves, stress concentration factors, weld classifications, current statistics and cyclic vessel-motion loads.
Lay vessel motion, deployment sequence, installation tension, buoyancy installation stages and connection procedures.
Vessel drift-off, emergency disconnect, loss of tension, extreme wave events and temporary installation configurations.
Minimum bend radius where applicable, allowable tension, bending stress, curvature, fatigue damage and connection load ratings.

outputs: Static riser configuration and spatial coordinates
Riser effective tension distribution along arc length
Axial forces, bending moments, shear forces and torsional response
Riser curvature, bend radius and maximum bending strain
Global riser displacements, velocities and accelerations
Dynamic top-tension and hang-off reaction histories
Vessel-motion-induced riser stresses and dynamic amplification
Vortex-induced vibration frequencies, response amplitudes and fatigue damage
Seabed contact forces, penetration and frictional resistance
Local buckling, external pressure collapse and combined-load utilization
Riser-to-riser clearances, interference risks and clashing locations
Hang-off connection forces, moments and utilization
Installation tension, deployment configuration and critical installation stages
Extreme storm response, disconnect response and safe operating limits
Local cross-sectional stress and strength checks
Remaining fatigue life, inspection-critical locations and integrity reports
subtitle: Steel catenary risers, top-tensioned risers, hybrid risers, drilling risers and other marine riser configurations.
ic: The initial conditions shall establish the riser configuration corresponding to its type, including steel catenary, top-tensioned, hybrid, flexible or drilling riser arrangements. The initial three-dimensional geometry shall include hang-off location, touchdown position, buoyancy modules, support interfaces and end connections.

The riser shall ordinarily begin from a converged static equilibrium under submerged weight, buoyancy, effective tension, internal fluid conditions and environmental loading. The initial axial force, bending moment, curvature and support reactions shall therefore be physically consistent with the starting geometry.

Dynamic simulations shall initialize riser displacements and velocities, vessel motions, top tension and seabed contact states. For a simulation beginning in calm conditions, the dynamic velocities may initially be zero after static equilibration. For simulations restarting from an operating history, the previous dynamic state shall be retained.

Internal flow simulations shall establish pressure, temperature, density, phase distribution and flow velocity along the riser. Fatigue studies shall include accumulated fatigue damage where available. Installation studies shall initialize the suspended length, departure angle, deployment tension and vessel position corresponding to the installation stage.
bc: The upper riser boundary shall represent the vessel or platform hang-off connection, including imposed translations, rotations, connection stiffness and possible prescribed top tension. Where a vessel-motion model is coupled to the riser, its motion shall be transferred continuously to the riser connection.

The lower boundary shall represent the actual seabed, wellhead, pipeline-end termination or other connection. For seabed-touchdown risers, contact conditions shall permit sliding, penetration resistance, friction and lift-off.

Hydrodynamic boundaries shall impose wave-induced water-particle motion, current velocity profiles, external hydrostatic pressure and appropriate hydrodynamic forces. Vortex-induced vibration analysis shall use relevant flow conditions and fluid-structure interaction assumptions.

Internal boundaries shall represent operating fluid pressure, temperature, flow rate and relevant pressure changes. End connections shall transfer appropriate axial forces, bending moments and torsion without introducing unintended restraints.

During installation, the boundaries shall prescribe vessel motion, top tension, lowering motion, installation support geometry and the evolving suspended configuration. Emergency-disconnect simulations shall modify connection constraints at the prescribed disconnection event and continue the resulting transient response.

calibration: Calibration should use instrumented riser measurements, offshore vessel motion records, laboratory riser dynamics experiments, towing-tank tests, hydrodynamic response tests and fatigue datasets.
Hydrodynamic drag, added mass and damping coefficients should be calibrated against measured riser vibration, displacement and force response under representative waves and currents.
Vortex-induced vibration parameters should be informed by controlled riser experiments and field data recording current profiles, oscillation frequencies, response modes and vibration amplitudes.
Riser axial stiffness, bending stiffness, effective tension and material damping should be calibrated using component testing and measured static or dynamic response.
Touchdown-zone soil interaction should be calibrated using laboratory pipe–soil tests, cyclic penetration experiments, friction measurements and observed seabed interaction.
Top-end connection stiffness and hang-off characteristics should be calibrated using component load tests and measured connection response.
Fatigue models should be calibrated using representative welded specimen tests, stress concentration measurements and recorded cyclic loading histories.
For top-tensioned and hybrid systems, tensioner performance, buoyancy properties and connector response should be calibrated using manufacturer testing and offshore monitoring where available.
verification: Static riser formulations should be verified against known suspended cable, catenary and tensioned-beam reference solutions.
Global force equilibrium, submerged weight, buoyancy and effective tension implementation should be checked across representative static configurations.
Dynamic riser solvers should undergo time-step and spatial discretization convergence studies, particularly for rapidly changing tension, bending and contact behaviour.
Wave and current load implementations should be checked using prescribed fluid velocities and independently calculated hydrodynamic force cases.
VIV response models should be tested against prescribed oscillatory loading, modal benchmarks and benchmark vibration problems.
Touchdown-zone contact should be verified for penetration, separation, frictional sliding and cyclic loading behaviour.
Buckling and collapse calculations should be checked against independent structural benchmarks, with mesh convergence for localized cross-sectional deformation.
Riser clashing and contact algorithms should be tested using controlled approach, collision and clearance cases.
Installation and deployment simulations should be checked through static and dynamic equilibrium, load continuity and convergence under successive deployment stages.
validation: Predicted static riser configurations and top tensions should be compared against independent measurements from installed riser systems or controlled experiments.
Dynamic displacements, accelerations, effective tensions and bending response should be compared with instrumented offshore or basin-test data.
VIV frequencies, amplitudes, mode shapes and fatigue damage should be assessed using independent experimental measurements.
Touchdown-zone movement, soil penetration and dynamic curvature should be validated using suitable laboratory or field data.
Connection load and hang-off response should be compared with physical component tests and measured operating reactions.
Buckling and collapse predictions should be evaluated against representative experimental structural tests.
Installation simulations should be assessed against recorded deployment tensions, vessel motions and installed configurations.
Fatigue life predictions should be evaluated through independent fatigue testing, long-term monitoring and documented inspection results.

geometry.text: Steel catenary risers, top-tensioned risers, hybrid risers, drilling risers, lazy-wave risers, steep-wave risers, riser towers, buoyancy modules, hang-off structures and touchdown-zone configurations.

geometry.cat: Conventional and universal CAD geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS, DXF and supported DWG should be accepted for riser pipes, connectors, bends, hang-off assemblies, stress joints, buoyancy modules, riser guides and local structural components.

geometry.cat: Riser centreline and global configuration formats
geometry.text: CSV, XYZ, JSON, XML, DXF three-dimensional polylines, GML and GeoJSON with suitable three-dimensional geometry should be supported for catenary shapes, lazy-wave profiles, global riser coordinates, elevation changes and touchdown locations. The software should reconstruct global beam or cable representations from centerline coordinates and assigned sectional properties.

Nastran BDF/NAS, Abaqus INP, Gmsh MSH, MED, UNV, VTK/VTU and Exodus should support compatible finite-element riser models, including beam elements, cross-sectional details, riser connectors and local solid models. Proprietary riser-analysis model formats may be supported through separately developed and validated adapters.

STL, OBJ, PLY, LAS/LAZ, E57, GeoTIFF, XYZ bathymetry, ESRI ASCII Grid and NetCDF-based gridded seabed geometry should be supported for vessel interface geometry, seabed contact modelling and irregular touchdown-zone reconstruction. Imported vessel motions and current profiles are supporting analysis data rather than geometry and should be handled separately from the geometry import process.
